The user can continue with a job ID and check later, and the render takes two minutes against a five-second timeout, so the export can leave the request. A successful run has three actors. The producer is the API: it publishes a message with the job ID and the export inputs, and it confirms that handoff before it tells the client the job was accepted. The broker holds the work for a worker. A publisher confirmation means the broker accepted the message under its durability rules; it is not the finished file. The worker receives the message, saves the file and a ready status, then acknowledges processing. That consumer acknowledgement lets the broker retire the delivery. The user learns completion by checking status, not from the accepted response.

A truthful accepted response is permitted by the confirmed handoff, the broker's acceptance, not by the file existing. The file is ready only when the worker has saved it and the status is ready. An accepted response is not the file. If processing later fails, the user needs a failed status that stays visible after the request ends. Report terminal failure rather than leaving the job looking accepted.

A login decision that must be final before access stays synchronous. The caller cannot continue without that result. Queueing the decision and granting access immediately would use a result the system does not yet have. Move work out of the request only when the caller can continue without its result.

One operating cost of the export queue is running the broker and the workers, along with status tracking, duplicate and retry handling, and backlog watching. The queue also does not remove a sustained overload.

The client checks that ID for pending, ready, or failed status. Only ready means the receipt can be used; an accepted response is not the receipt.
This shortens the initial wait, not the work itself. It adds delayed results, status tracking, and failures that must remain visible after the request ends.

Trace publish → broker acceptance → worker effect → consumer acknowledgement. The client observes completion through status.
Isolate it, or any job that exhausts its budget, in a dead-letter queue for investigation and expose failed status.
Authorization must finish before showing a private receipt. Queueing the decision and granting access immediately would use a result we do not yet have.

Receipt generation can be deferred if the caller accepts a job ID and later status. Confirm the handoff before acceptance; report ready only after the required result is saved, and expose terminal failure.
The tradeoff includes operating the broker and workers, tracking status, handling duplicates and retries, and watching backlog. A queue does not solve sustained overload.

The worker already committed the credit, then crashed before acknowledging. With at-least-once delivery, the broker may deliver that same job again. The next worker can try to credit the balance a second time.

Acknowledging before the credit is unsafe in the other direction. If the worker acknowledges first and then crashes before saving the credit, the broker can retire the delivery and the credit is lost.

Make the credit idempotent with a stable business-operation ID reused across retries, not a new ID per attempt. Repeating the operation then has the same effect as doing it once. In one database transaction, insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the balance credit. Commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the credit. A separate check followed by a write can race or crash between the two steps, so the duplicate-detection record and the credit have to commit together.

This does not establish universal exactly-once message delivery. The transaction protects those database effects. It does not make an external payment atomic with the message, and neither the publisher confirmation nor the consumer acknowledgement makes a broker operation atomic with the database write.

evidence.quote: Neither makes a broker operation atomic with a database write or proves an arbitrary business effect succeeded.

A worker commits its database changes, then crashes before acknowledging. With at-least-once delivery, the broker can deliver the job again. Acknowledging first instead risks losing the work if the worker crashes before saving it.
Repeating the same operation has the same effect as doing it once. Reuse a stable business-operation ID across retries, not a new ID per attempt.

In one database transaction, insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the receipt changes. Commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the effect. A separate check followed by a write can race or crash between steps.
That transaction protects its database effects. It does not make an external email or payment atomic, or turn delivery into a universal exactly-once guarantee.
Expect repeated delivery; make the effect duplicate-safe at its own boundary.

The unreachable image store is a temporary problem that may recover. Retry that message with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget. Immediate retries can deepen the outage. If the budget is exhausted, stop retrying and isolate the job in a dead-letter queue for investigation, and expose failed status.

The unsupported file format will not improve with waiting. Do not keep retrying it. Isolate it in the dead-letter queue and expose failed status.

Healthy jobs keep moving; the isolated job does not block them. A dead-letter queue contains the failure. It does not repair the job.

Before someone deliberately replays an isolated job, fix the cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect. The replay still needs duplicate safety.

The events are delivered in order, set quantity to 5 and then set quantity to 2, but the second write finishes first. The slower update to 5 can finish last and overwrite 2, so the stored quantity ends at 5. That is the wrong final quantity: the later event said 2. Starting first does not mean finishing first, and ordered delivery alone does not guarantee ordered effects.

Serialize effects for this item ID. Keep the update to 2 waiting while the update to 5 runs or retries. Apply 5, then apply 2, so the dependency is preserved. Different items can still run at the same time.

The throughput cost is that one busy item becomes a bottleneck: its updates cannot run in parallel with each other. If the earlier update is moved to a dead-letter queue, that does not resolve the dependency. Decide how to repair or cancel it before releasing the later update.

evidence.quote: Two updates change one receipt's address: old, then new. Workers receive them in order, but the slower old update finishes last and overwrites new.
Serialize effects per receipt ID: keep later updates waiting while an earlier one runs or retries. Different receipts can still run in parallel. A busy receipt becomes a throughput bottleneck.
Moving the earlier job to a dead-letter queue does not resolve the dependency. Decide how to repair or cancel it before releasing dependent updates.
Ordered delivery alone does not guarantee ordered effects.

If 120 jobs arrive each second and 80 finish, unfinished work grows by 40 jobs per second. The same subtraction the lesson uses for 100 arrivals and 70 completions growing by 30 applies here: 120 minus 80 is 40. That growth continues for as long as these rates continue.

Growing oldest-job age means the wait for the oldest thumbnail is getting longer. That growing wait can violate the promise to the client. Storage and retention are also finite. A queue can absorb a burst only if capacity later catches up before those limits or the allowed delay are reached. It does not create unlimited capacity, and it should not hide a sustained overload.

The image store is already at its safe concurrency limit, so do not add workers to push more concurrent work at it. Bound worker concurrency to stay inside that limit. At the producer, throttle or reject new requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer them only within an agreed limit. Control arrivals and the downstream work.

More workers would help only when the workers are the bottleneck and the downstream image store has spare capacity. When that downstream is already saturated, more workers increase contention instead.

evidence.quote: If 100 receipt jobs arrive each second and 70 finish, unfinished work grows by 30 jobs per second. Watch backlog and oldest-job age: a growing wait can violate the promise to the client.

Bound worker concurrency to protect the database. Throttle or reject new requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer them within an agreed limit.
More workers help when workers are the bottleneck and downstream services have spare capacity. If the database is already saturated, more workers increase contention instead.
Control arrivals and downstream work; do not hide sustained overload in a growing queue.
A queue buys time, not unlimited capacity

Billing and analytics each need every purchase event, and analytics must replay the last day, so a single work queue is the wrong shape. A work queue divides jobs among competing workers. It does not give every independent application every job. One pool of competing workers would split purchases between consumers, and a consumer that takes a job removes it from the others. Failed deliveries can still repeat.

Use a retained log, such as Kafka, with a billing consumer group and an analytics consumer group. Each group receives every purchase event. A partition is an ordered slice of the log. Workers inside one group share that group's partitions, so billing's workers divide the partitions among themselves and analytics' workers do the same for their own group. Each group tracks its own position, an offset, for each partition. The two groups do not share one position.

Committing an offset records that group's progress. It does not delete the event. Analytics can rewind and replay the last day only while those events remain under the retention policy. If retention has already dropped them, the replay is not available.

Adding partitions or consumers does not create one global order or exactly-once external effects. Ordering is per partition, not across all partitions. Retained history and offsets do not by themselves make external effects exactly once.

evidence.quote: A work queue divides receipt jobs among competing workers; it does not give every independent application every job. Failed deliveries can still repeat.

If receipts and analytics each need every purchase event, a retained log such as Kafka supports separate consumer groups. A partition is an ordered slice of the log. Each group tracks its own position, called an offset, for each partition. Workers within a group share the partitions.
Committing an offset records progress; it does not delete the event. Analytics can rewind and replay only while the required events remain under the retention policy.
Ordering is per partition, not global across all partitions. Retained history and offsets do not by themselves make external effects exactly once.
Choose job distribution for shared work, or independent group positions and retained history when applications need replay.
